name: tail-recursion
intent: Express an iterative computation as a recursive function whose recursive call is the last action, so the runtime can reuse the frame - or a mechanical rewrite can turn the call into a loop - and the algorithm keeps recursion's declarative shape without growing the stack.
problem: A computation that is naturally 'do one step, then start over' - consuming a token stream, retrying, iterating a state machine - is written as recursion because that is how the problem reads, but every step allocates a frame: deep inputs overflow the stack, and per-step cost is higher than the loop the algorithm really is. The usual workaround, hand-converting the recursion into a loop with reassigned locals, loses the case-by-case readability and has to be repeated for every such function.
context: Applies when control flow is genuinely iterative and the recursive call can be put in tail position: lexers and protocol readers, retry/backoff loops, state machines, accumulating traversals, CPS-style interpreters, numeric iteration. What the pattern delivers depends on the toolchain - languages with a tail-call guarantee or a checking annotation can leave the recursion in place, while JVM, CLR, CPython, Go and MRI programs must make the loop explicit. It also requires that nothing consume the call's result: no accumulator arithmetic after the call, no cons, no cleanup or release.
benefits: Constant stack for an iterative process: the recursion costs the same stack space as the loop it stands for, so depth is bounded by the data rather than by the runtime's frame budget.
Keeps the recursive formulation in the source: the cases stay cases and the accumulator argument makes the carried state explicit instead of dissolving the algorithm into reassignment.
The step becomes a total transition (state, input) -> state, which is directly testable and stays reentrant as long as the state travels in parameters.

Where the toolchain guarantees or checks the elimination (Kotlin tailrec, Scala @tailrec, Clang musttail, Rust become, Scheme-style proper tail calls), a de-optimized call is a build error or an explicit promise rather than a latent overflow.
Often cheaper than ordinary recursion even when the frame is reused: fewer frame allocations and better locality, because the same frame is overwritten step after step.
tradeoffs: Silent de-optimization in best-effort toolchains (C, C++, Rust release builds, Swift): one edit that consumes the call's result, another optimization level or another compiler turns a bounded iteration back into an unbounded recursion with no diagnostic.

Tail position is fragile: any work after the call - an accumulator cons, arithmetic, a finally/scope-exit action, an ARC release, a destructor - removes the tail call, and outside the checking languages nothing reports it.
Debuggability drops: eliminated frames vanish from stack traces and profilers, so recursion depth, call path and per-step state are invisible exactly where the pattern is used.
The accumulator rewrite drifts from the published recursive specification; reviews and proofs must re-establish the invariant, and readers translate between two shapes of the same algorithm.
No asymptotic gain by itself: the number of steps is unchanged, so the pattern never replaces memoisation or a better algorithm - it only removes the O(depth) stack.
With the base case missing or unreachable, an eliminated tail call loops forever where ordinary recursion would at least crash at a limit.

participants.responsibility: Computes one step and delegates the rest of the work to a call in tail position, carrying all state in its parameters.
Carries the work already done into the next call, so that nothing has to be done after the call returns.
Recognizes the terminal state and returns the result without a further call; the only exit from the loop.
The last action of the function - the position the optimizer replaces with a jump, or the rewrite replaces with an assignment plus continue.
Eliminates the frame: a language guarantee, a compiler-checked annotation, or the programmer's explicit conversion to a loop. Its presence or absence decides whether the pattern holds.

use_cases: Tokenisers, lexers and byte-oriented protocol readers that consume one unit per step and re-enter with the remainder.
Retry and backoff loops and polling state machines: attempt, adjust the state, and re-enter until the terminal state.
Accumulating traversals - sums, folds, reachability walks - expressed as a step function with the accumulator in a parameter.
Interpreters and CPS evaluators, where every step is a tail call and elimination (or a trampoline) is what keeps them finite.
Numeric iteration such as fixed-point and Newton-style loops, where the next iterate is the recursive call's only argument.

Erlang/OTP: BEAM process loops - receive loops and long-lived worker loops written as tail-recursive functions - rely on the documented last-call optimization: the reference manual states a call at the end of a function body reuses the current stack frame, so a tail-recursive loop can run forever without exhausting the process stack.

Lua: the reference manual guarantees proper tail calls - a function invoked as return f(x) (outside any to-be-closed variable scope) reuses the caller's stack frame, so interpreter-style dispatch loops written this way have no fixed nesting-depth limit.

F# on .NET: recursion replaces loops because the compiler emits .NET tail calls (or compiles the function into a loop), making recursive list walks as cheap as while loops; the docs enumerate what silently blocks the emission - try/finally regions and the --tailcalls switch, off by default in Visual Studio Debug builds.
avoid_when: The recursion is not in tail position and cannot be made so without restructuring (tree folds, divide and conquer): use ordinary recursion, the language's fold, or a trampoline.
Mutual recursion is required: self-recursion-only elimination does not cover it - use a trampoline or an explicit state machine.
Depth is small and bounded by the input shape: plain recursion is clearer and the elimination does not matter.
The toolchain offers no elimination and the loop reads just as well: write the loop or use the standard fold/iterator instead of encoding a loop in recursion.
anti_patterns: Assuming elimination: writing the recursion because 'compilers optimize tail calls' in a runtime that does not (JVM, CLR, CPython, Go, MRI, V8) and shipping a stack overflow on deep input.
Accumulating in captured mutable state - a closure variable, a field, a global - instead of a parameter: the step stops being reentrant and the loop becomes shared state.
Mechanically rewriting every recursion as tail recursion, including naturally structural ones (folds over trees), producing accumulators that hide the algorithm.
Missing or unreachable base case: with the frames eliminated the bug presents as a hang or an endless loop instead of a stack overflow.
Hand-written tail recursion that re-implements a standard fold or iterator the language already provides.
design_principles: Single responsibility: one step per function; iteration is the repetition of a total state transition.
Explicit state: the accumulator parameter replaces hidden mutable variables, which is what makes the transformation verifiable.
Mechanical sympathy: state the algorithm in the shape the runtime actually executes (a jump) instead of relying on an unstated compiler promise.
Behaviour preservation: the rewrite is correct only if the accumulator invariant reproduces the original recursion's result for every input.
Purity and reentrancy: a step function that depends on nothing but its parameters can be tested and run concurrently without further thought.
best_practices: Check tail position mechanically: nothing may consume the call's result - no arithmetic, no consing into a structure, no try/catch or finally, no cleanup or destructor work after the call.
Carry all state in parameters and document the accumulator invariant; that invariant is what the tests should assert.
Use the toolchain's checker where one exists (Kotlin tailrec, Scala @tailrec, Clang [[clang::musttail]], Rust become) so that losing the tail call fails the build or is an explicit promise.
Reserve the pattern for recursions that are genuinely iterative; structural recursion belongs to a fold or an explicit work stack.
Bound the iteration independently: an eliminated tail call has no stack limit to stop it, so the loop needs its own progress argument or counter.
Prefer the standard fold or iterator when it expresses the same accumulation; hand-written tail recursion is the fallback when it does not.
sources: Guy L. Steele Jr. & Gerald Jay Sussman, Lambda: The Ultimate Imperative (MIT AI Memo 353, March 1976) - the origin of modelling iteration and jumps as tail calls; http://hdl.handle.net/1721.1/5790

Harold Abelson & Gerald Jay Sussman, Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs (MIT Press, 2nd ed. 1996), section 1.2.1 'Linear Recursion and Iteration' - the accumulator argument for expressing an iterative process as a tail-recursive procedure.

Design Patterns in Functional Programming, 'Tail Recursion' - the pattern as a functional-catalog entry (intent, forces, consequences); https://dev.to/mrcaidev/design-patterns-in-functional-programming-4aah
Wikipedia, 'Tail call' - tail-call elimination, language support, and the JVM/JavaScript history; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tail_call
Guido van Rossum, 'Tail Recursion Elimination' (2009) - why CPython deliberately refuses the transformation; https://neopythonic.blogspot.com/2009/04/tail-recursion-elimination.html

Erlang/OTP, 'Functions' reference manual, 'Tail recursion' - the BEAM's documented last-call optimization: a call in tail position reuses the stack frame, enabling tail-recursive loops without stack growth; https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/ref_man_functions.html

Erlang/OTP, 'The Seven Myths of Erlang Performance' - myth that tail-recursive functions are always faster than body-recursive ones; since R12B memory usage is similar and body recursion often wins, so elimination is a safety property, not a default speed win; https://erlang.org/documentation/doc-15.0-rc1/doc/system/myths.html

Lua 5.4 Reference Manual - proper tail calls: return f(x) outside to-be-closed scopes reuses the caller's stack frame with no fixed nesting-depth limit, at the cost of debug information about the calling function; https://www.lua.org/manual/5.4/manual.html

F# Team, 'Tail calls in F#' (Microsoft Learn) - when the compiler emits a .NET tail call or compiles recursion into a loop, and the documented blockers: try/finally, calls returning unit through first-class function values, and --tailcalls disabled by default in Debug builds; https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/fsharpteam/tail-calls-in-f

Revised^7 Report on the Algorithmic Language Scheme, 'Proper tail recursion' - the normative requirement that implementations support an unbounded number of active tail calls, with tail contexts defined inductively per lambda; https://standards.scheme.org/corrected-r7rs/r7rs-Z-H-5.html
